content: In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), there is a significant need for further research on interventions addressing suicide prevention. Only one randomized controlled trial (RCT) was identified that included data on the critical outcome of death by suicide, but it lacked sufficient statistical power to detect an effect. Additional studies focusing on suicide-related outcomes are urgently required. The implementation of digital interventions for mental health involves costs primarily associated with the technical development, establishment, and maintenance of online platforms. Stand-alone digital interventions, such as those based on evidence-based therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), problem-solving therapy (PST), and mindfulness, should be considered as supportive tools for individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts. However, the strength of this recommendation is conditional, and the certainty of evidence supporting it is low. When delivering digital interventions, it is essential to consider user preferences for human versus digital contact and the variability in access to digital platforms across different regions. A digital divide exists, with some population groups facing unequal access to network services, mobile devices, electricity, and digital literacy. Additionally, country-specific adaptation and translation of digital tools, followed by evaluation, are critical for effective implementation. The guideline, developed in English, will have its executive summary translated into all six official WHO languages. Updated or new recommendations will be accessible online, along with detailed evidence profiles, GRADE tables, and considerations regarding user preferences, values, and feasibility. Ministries of health will be informed of the updated guideline through WHO regional and country offices. A briefing package, including an executive summary and a Q&A document, will be prepared for technical officers outside WHO headquarters, highlighting key updates and new recommendations. The media will also be notified of the updated guideline. Capacity-building activities will be conducted through regional and subregional meetings and other initiatives related to the Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) and the implementation of WHO’s action plans, including the Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2021–2030, the Intersectoral Global Action Plan on Epilepsy and Neurological Disorders 2022–2031, the Global Action Plan on Dementia 2017–2025, and the Global Alcohol Action Plan 2022–2030. Derivative products based on the mhGAP guideline will be revised to reflect updates and incorporated into the mhGAP Intervention Guide (mhGAP-IG). This guide translates evidence-based recommendations into simple clinical protocols and algorithms for use by non-specialist health workers in primary and secondary healthcare settings. It also serves as a resource for healthcare planners and program managers working in alignment with WHO’s Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2030. The guideline will also be integrated into other mhGAP materials, such as the mhGAP Humanitarian Intervention Guide (mhGAP-HIG), the mhGAP-IG App (e-mhGAP), training manuals, operations manuals, community toolkits, and an e-learning course being developed with the WHO Academy. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) and its pediatric counterpart (EMLc) include products for mental, neurological, and substance use (MNS) disorders. Updated recommendations for psychotropic medicines will inform the EML and EMLc to promote affordable access to quality, safe, and effective medications for MNS disorders. WHO will monitor and evaluate the impact of the guideline by collecting regular feedback from implementation activities, international experts, and health workers familiar with the mhGAP guideline. Existing WHO resources, such as the Mental Health Atlas and action plans, will support this evaluation. The guideline will be updated five years after publication. The WHO Steering Group will monitor research developments in mhGAP module areas, particularly for questions with no evidence or low-certainty evidence, to determine whether new recommendations or changes to existing ones are warranted. Any concerns about the validity of recommendations will be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for updates.
